parts.label: (a)
parts.text: With reference to velocity and acceleration, describe uniform circular motion.
hints: Hint 1: Think carefully about the word uniform. What stays the same and what must be changing when an object moves in a circle?
Hint 2: If velocity is changing, there must be acceleration. Which direction must it act to keep the object on a circle without speeding it up or slowing it down?
parts.proper_answer: Speed is constant (magnitude of velocity constant). Velocity direction changes continuously, tangential to the circle. Acceleration is towards the centre of the circle, perpendicular to velocity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate Speed From Velocity**
You are sitting beside me watching a car go round steadily. Its speedometer does not move, so speed is constant. But velocity is a vector. In a circle the direction of motion is always changing, always pointing along the tangent. So velocity is continuously changing even though speed is not. That is the key idea in uniform circular motion.

Step 2: **Get The Acceleration Direction Right**
Changing velocity means there is acceleration. For the speed to stay constant, this acceleration must do no work along the motion, so it must act at $90^{\circ}$ to the velocity at every instant. That direction is radially inwards, towards the centre of the circle. We call it centripetal acceleration: $$a = \frac{v^2}{r}$$ directed towards the centre, perpendicular to velocity.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
Two cars are moving around a horizontal circular track. One car follows path X and the other follows path Y, as shown in Fig. 1.1.
{{figure:figure_1_1}}
Fig. 1.1 (not to scale)
The radius of path X is $318\text{ m}$. Path Y is parallel to, and $27\text{ m}$ outside, path X. Both cars have mass $790\text{ kg}$. The maximum lateral (sideways) friction force $F$ that the cars can experience without sliding is the same for both cars.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text:
The maximum speed at which the car on path X can move around the track without sliding is $94\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Calculate $F$.

markscheme_points.text: $F = mv^2 / r$ or $v = r\omega$ and $F = mr\omega^2$

hints: Hint 1: What force keeps the car on the circle? At maximum speed without sliding, the sideways friction must be providing all the required centripetal force.
Hint 2: Link that friction force $F$ to the known $m$, $v$ and $r$ for path X, then check your units and give the answer to 2 or 3 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify The Centripetal Force**
To stay on path X the car needs a resultant force towards the centre. Here that can only come from lateral friction from the tyres. At the limit, $F$ equals the required centripetal force: $$F = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$ where $m = 790\text{ kg}$, $v = 94\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $r = 318\text{ m}$.

Step 2: **Substitute And Calculate**
Put the numbers in before any rearranging is needed: $$F = \frac{790 \times (94)^2}{318}$$ $$F = \frac{790 \times 8836}{318} \approx 2.20 \times 10^4\text{ N}$$ So $F \approx 2.2 \times 10^4\text{ N}$. This is the maximum sideways friction available to both cars.

parts.text:
Both cars move around the track. Each car has the maximum speed at which it can move without sliding.

markscheme_points.text: time taken for one lap of the track: greater

hints: Hint 1: Both cars have the same mass and the same limiting friction $F$. What does $a = F/m$ tell you about their centripetal accelerations at maximum speed?
Hint 2: Path Y has larger radius $r$. If $F = mv^2/r$ stays fixed, how must $v^2$ change to compensate for larger $r$?
Hint 3: For the lap time, think of $T = \text{distance}/\text{speed} = 2\pi r / v$. Both $r$ and $v$ are larger for Y, but which effect wins? Try writing $T$ in terms of $r$ only.
parts.proper_answer: centripetal acceleration: Y same as X. maximum speed: Y greater than X. time taken for one lap: Y greater than X.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Centripetal Acceleration Is The Same**
At maximum speed, centripetal acceleration is $a = F/m$. Both $F$ and $m$ are identical for the two cars, so $$a_Y = a_X$$ The larger radius of Y does not change this because $F$ is the limiting factor.

Step 2: **Maximum Speed Is Greater For Y**
From $F = mv^2/r$ we get: $$v = \sqrt{\frac{Fr}{m}}$$ With $F$ and $m$ fixed, $v$ is proportional to $\sqrt{r}$. Path Y has $r_Y = 318 + 27 = 345\text{ m}$, larger than $r_X$. So the car on Y can go faster before $mv^2/r$ reaches the limit $F$. Hence $v_Y > v_X$.

Step 3: **Lap Time Is Greater For Y**
Lap time is distance over speed: $$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v}$$ Substitute $v = \sqrt{Fr/m}$ to get: $$T = \frac{2\pi r}{\sqrt{Fr/m}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{mr}{F}}$$ So $T$ is proportional to $\sqrt{r}$. Larger $r$ means larger $T$, even though $v$ is also larger, because distance grows as $r$ while speed only grows as $\sqrt{r}$. Hence $T_Y > T_X$.
